Stated Claim / Post Context:
Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is in Solitary 24 Hours Daily After Publicly Calling For Trump’s Impeachment

Maj. Jason Watson has been jailed since August after publicly opining on the president and his administration, drawing a big legal battle.

Actual Article Body:
Maj. Jason Watson has been jailed since August after publicly opining on the president and his administration, drawing a big legal battle.

A U.S. Air Force member jailed since August for publicly calling for President Donald Trump's impeachment is being held in solitary confinement 24 hours a day, according to his attorney.

Watson was arrested July 1 on the steps of the U.S. Capitol, where he demonstrated in uniform with a sign reading "Impeach. Convict. Remove." after speaking at a news conference calling for Trump's removal.

On Aug. 18, one day after he repeated his criticism in a CNN interview, the Air Force ordered him into pretrial confinement, saying at the time that he was being held at a county facility in Maryland on a military hold.

Maj. Jason Watson is "still in solitary confinement 24 hours a day," his attorney, Christopher Mutimer, told CNN on Friday, Oct. 9.

"Even if he gets an hour to eat or to exercise, he's alone," Mutimer said. "He's looking at having his liberty potentially taken away. ... He is looking at being removed from the military, losing his benefits and potentially spending significant time in jail."

The Air Force and Mutimer did not respond to Military.com's request for comment on Watson's confinement conditions.

Prosecutors charged Watson under three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), including the rarely used Article 88, which bars officers from using "contemptuous words" against the president.

The government also moved toward trying him at a general court-martial, the military's most serious level of trial.

Military law draws a hard line in cases such as this.

Article 13 of the UCMJ prohibits punishing a service member who is awaiting trial and says confinement may not be "any more rigorous than the circumstances require."

Courts-martial can award credit against an eventual sentence when a judge finds pretrial confinement crossed the line into punishment. When the Air Force first confined Watson in August, it cited "probable cause to support allegations of continued misconduct."

They said he "is presumed innocent and will be afforded all rights" under the military rule that requires his confinement to be reviewed.

The service has not publicly addressed Mutimer's description of the conditions.

Mutimer told CNN the government is moving forward with a general court-martial, the military equivalent of a civilian felony trial.

In September, a hearing officer recommended that most charges proceed to that forum while urging that several others be dismissed, as Military.com previously reported.

The Air Force has not publicly confirmed that the convening authority—the commander who makes the final call—has formally referred the case to trial.

Watson's defense has asked for the charges to be handled instead at a special court-martial, a less severe forum, and has compared his case to that of Marine Lt. Col. Stuart Scheller.

Scheller was court-martialed after publicly criticizing military leaders over the Afghanistan withdrawal and pleaded guilty to lesser charges.

Watson has framed his protest as a matter of conscience rather than politics.

"Nothing that is worth doing is something that you can do for free. Everything that is worthwhile is going to cost something," he told CNN in an interview recorded before his arrest.

"So, all that I could do was ask myself, what's the highest price that I'm willing to pay?" Watson added.

No trial date has been set as Watson remains in pretrial confinement.

Ilhan Omar (D-MN), with several arguing that the criminal probe shattered a critical, longstanding norm.“The Trump [Justice Department] tears up yet another long-standing policy/norm, this one of refusi...

Actual Article Body:
Journalists and legal experts reacted with disgust Monday to the federal raid on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN), with several arguing that the criminal probe shattered a critical, longstanding norm.

“The Trump [Justice Department] tears up yet another long-standing policy/norm, this one of refusing to take actions like this before an election,” noted Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration attorney and senior fellow at the American Immigration Council.

“[Attorney General Todd] Blanche, when he was Trump's lawyer, argued that so long as a candidacy was declared, no such action should occur. Now, it's 3 weeks from an election.”

Federal agents executed a search warrant early Monday on Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., as part of a criminal investigation, but “provided no other details,” the Associated Press reported.

President Donald Trump has previously alleged, without evidence, that Omar, a U.S. citizen, was in the country “illegally,” and that she should be thrown “the hell out.” Such claims have led to speculation that the raid and related criminal probe were related to Omar’s citizenship status, though Reichlin-Melnick argued such a case would be on shaky legal ground.

“An important bit of immigration law relevant here; Section 212(k) of the INA already creates a waiver by which immigrants who obtain status through fraud that they didn't know about can avoid consequences like losing a green card,” he wrote in a follow-up post on social media. “So this is *even weaker* than it already seems.”

Joyce Vance, legal expert and former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, argued that the raid represented “another hard norm out the window” given its proximity to the midterms next month. Writer Jim Stewartson, in response to the raid, called the Trump administration a “sick racist regime,” and journalist Mikey Smith of the Daily Mirror similarly called the raid “racist political intimidation.”

“Raiding a member of congress's home to search for immigration paperwork filled out decades ago by her now-deceased father really checks all the fascist police state boxes,” wrote Tommy Vietor, former Obama administration official and podcaster.

After SCOTUS Setback, Trump Renews Bid To Remove Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook

'As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law.'

Actual Article Body:
‘As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law.’

President Trump has launched a probe into Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook over mortgage fraud allegations, the White House announced Friday. The move appears aimed at removing Cook from the post following an unfavorable Supreme Court ruling on the matter earlier this year.

“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in Friday’s presidential memoranda.

The directive establishes a committee comprised of the president’s assistant for economic policy, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission chair, and the director of the Office of Government Ethics that will investigate allegations that Cook, a Biden appointee, “made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments.” The group will subsequently report to the president “whether there is ’cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal within the meaning” of federal law “as construed” in the Supreme Court’s Trump v. Cook (2026) decision.

Trump first sought to fire Cook over these allegations in August 2025, but was blocked by D.C. District Judge Jib Cobb, a Biden appointee. The administration ultimately filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to temporarily permit Cook’s removal while litigation over her firing continued. The high court rejected the government’s request in Trump v. Cook.

Writing for the 5-4 majority, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled there must be “cause” to fire Cook, and she must be afforded an “opportunity to respond to the charges made against her … [before] a final decision [can] be made.” The majority declined to rule on “the ultimate question” of whether Trump can remove Cook “for cause,” arguing such a decision “will depend in part on the underlying facts” that must first “be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards.”

The court’s decision prompted stinging dissents from Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito (joined by Neil Gorsuch), and Amy Coney Barrett. Thomas noted “[a]pparent mortgage fraud was a ’cause’ to remove Cook” and underscored a point he raised during oral arguments — that “the statute authorizing the President to remove Cook for ’cause’ says nothing about notice or a hearing, so it does not require notice and a hearing.” The senior justice also argued the federal courts lack the authority to “enter the relief” the Cook majority upheld with its decision and further admonished the majority for infringing on the president’s executive removal powers.

Alito (and Gorsuch) argued that Trump showed a likelihood of success on the preliminary questions of whether “for cause” removal applies to pre-office conduct and whether he violated Cook’s due process rights. Meanwhile, Barrett blasted the majority for deciding significant legal matters that had not been fully briefed or contested, as well as the “disconnect between its holding and its disposition line.”

[READ: John Roberts: Presidents Have Executive Power. Also John Roberts: No, They Don’t]

Following the constraints established in Cook, Trump has directed the newly formed committee to “conduct an in-person hearing to consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook” on Nov. 5. The hearing will last “no longer than 4 hours,” according to the memoranda.

The directive also grants Cook the ability to file a written statement with the committee contesting the allegations, so long as it is submitted at least three days in advance. While the Biden appointee will be given the opportunity to “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations,” the committee will be afforded the chance to “question Governor Cook about any representations she or her counsel make during the hearing, or it may authorize its representatives, including Department of Justice personnel, to conduct that questioning.”

Cook and her team will be presented the evidence against her prior to the hearing. The committee may also request Cook turn over “documents or other evidentiary submissions … as appropriate,” which Cook is instructed to comply with. The hearing will not be broadcast to the public “but shall be transcribed,” according to the directive.
